## Variables & Assignments

```{=html}
<div class="ref-section">
<h3>Assigning values</h3>
```

Use `<-` or `=` to assign a value to a variable. R is **case-sensitive** — `hello` and `Hello` are different objects.

```r
a   <- 2            # numeric
b   <- TRUE         # logical
name <- "Rosalinde" # character (string)

a + 3               # use in calculations: returns 5
print(name)         # explicitly print to console
```

```{=html}
<table class="fn-table">
  <tr><th>Function</th><th>What it does</th></tr>
  <tr><td>str(x)</td><td>Show structure and type of x</td></tr>
  <tr><td>ls()</td><td>List all objects in the environment</td></tr>
  <tr><td>rm(x)</td><td>Remove variable x from the environment</td></tr>
  <tr><td>load("file.RData")</td><td>Reload a saved environment</td></tr>
</table>
</div>
```

## Vectors

```{=html}
<div class="ref-section">
<h3>Creating &amp; accessing vectors</h3>
```

A vector is a sequence of values of the **same type**. When you mix types, R converts everything to the lowest common type (logical → numeric → character).

```r
y <- c(9, 3, 7, 2)   # numeric vector of length 4
length(y)             # 4

# Indexing
y[3]          # 7        — third element
y[2:4]        # 3 7 2    — elements 2 to 4
y[-2]         # 9 7 2    — all except element 2
y[y < 5]      # 3 2      — elements where condition is TRUE

# Logical tests (applied to each element)
y < 5         # FALSE TRUE FALSE TRUE
sum(y < 5)    # 2  — count of elements satisfying condition

# Modifying
y[1] <- 10    # replace first element
```

```{=html}
<div class="tip-box">
  <strong>TRUE / FALSE in arithmetic:</strong> R treats <code>TRUE</code> as 1 and <code>FALSE</code> as 0.
  So <code>sum(c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE))</code> = 3 — a quick way to count matching elements.
</div>
</div>
```

## Matrices

```{=html}
<div class="ref-section">
<h3>Creating &amp; accessing matrices</h3>
```

A matrix is a **2-dimensional** structure. All elements must be the same type. Indexing uses `[row, column]` — leave one side empty to select all.

```r
X <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 2, ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)
#      [,1] [,2] [,3]
# [1,]    1    2    3
# [2,]    4    5    6

dim(X)        # c(2, 3)  — rows, then columns
X[1, 2]       # 2        — row 1, column 2
X[2, ]        # 4 5 6    — entire second row
X[, 1]        # 1 4      — entire first column

# Building from vectors
A <- cbind(c(1,2), c(3,4), c(5,6))   # join as columns
B <- rbind(c(1,2,3), c(4,5,6))       # join as rows

# Naming
rownames(A) <- c("r1", "r2")
colnames(A) <- c("p1", "p2", "p3")
```

```{=html}
<table class="fn-table">
  <tr><th>Function</th><th>What it does</th></tr>
  <tr><td>dim(X)</td><td>Returns c(rows, columns)</td></tr>
  <tr><td>nrow(X) / ncol(X)</td><td>Number of rows / columns</td></tr>
  <tr><td>cbind(x, y)</td><td>Combine vectors as columns</td></tr>
  <tr><td>rbind(x, y)</td><td>Combine vectors as rows</td></tr>
  <tr><td>colnames(X)</td><td>Get or set column names</td></tr>
  <tr><td>rownames(X)</td><td>Get or set row names</td></tr>
</table>
</div>
```

## Lists

```{=html}
<div class="ref-section">
<h3>Creating &amp; accessing lists</h3>
```

Lists can hold **elements of different types and lengths** — unlike vectors or matrices. Access elements with `$name` or `[[ ]]`.

```r
L <- list(color = c("blue", "red"), size = 5, active = TRUE)

# Accessing content (returns the actual value)
L$color           # "blue" "red"
L[["color"]]      # same — "blue" "red"
L[["color"]][2]   # "red"

# Single brackets return a list, not the content
L["color"]        # a list of length 1 (not the vector!)
length(L["color"])   # 1
length(L[["color"]]) # 2

# Modifying & deleting
L[["size"]] <- 10     # change an element
L[["new"]]  <- "hi"   # add a new element
L[[3]] <- NULL         # delete third element
```

```{=html}
<div class="tip-box">
  <strong>[ ] vs [[ ]]:</strong> Single brackets always return a <em>list</em>.
  Double brackets return the <em>content</em>. Use <code>[[ ]]</code> when you want to work with the value.
</div>
</div>
```

## Dataframes

```{=html}
<div class="ref-section">
<h3>Creating &amp; accessing dataframes</h3>
```

A dataframe is like a table: rows are observations, columns are variables. Unlike matrices, **different columns can have different types**.

```r
Name   <- c("Ben", "Alice", "Daniel", "Charlie")
Year   <- c(1990, 1992, 1995, 1993)
Option <- c("Biology", "Physics", "Chemistry", "Mathematics")

df <- data.frame(First_Name = Name, Year = Year, Options = Option)

# Accessing columns
df$Year           # 1990 1992 1995 1993
df[["Year"]]      # same
df[, 2]           # same — all rows, column 2

# Accessing elements
df$Options[3]     # "Chemistry"
df[2:3, 3]        # "Physics" "Chemistry"

# Merging two dataframes
Full_Names <- data.frame(First_Name = c("Alice","Ben"),
                         Last_Name  = c("Parker","James"))

merge(df, Full_Names)          # Inner join — only matching rows
merge(df, Full_Names, all=TRUE) # Outer join — all rows, NA for missing
```

```{=html}
<table class="fn-table">
  <tr><th>Function</th><th>What it does</th></tr>
  <tr><td>data.frame(...)</td><td>Create a dataframe from named vectors</td></tr>
  <tr><td>as.data.frame(X)</td><td>Convert a matrix to a dataframe</td></tr>
  <tr><td>dim(df)</td><td>Rows and columns</td></tr>
  <tr><td>colnames(df)</td><td>Column names</td></tr>
  <tr><td>str(df)</td><td>Structure overview (types, first values)</td></tr>
  <tr><td>merge(a, b)</td><td>Join two dataframes on shared columns</td></tr>
</table>
</div>
```

## Loops & Iteration

```{=html}
<div class="ref-section">
<h3>apply family &amp; for loops</h3>
```

```r
Mat <- matrix(rnorm(12), nrow = 3)

apply(Mat, 1, mean)   # mean of each ROW    (MARGIN = 1)
apply(Mat, 2, mean)   # mean of each COLUMN (MARGIN = 2)

x <- c(1:5)
sapply(x, sqrt)       # apply sqrt() to each element → returns vector
lapply(x, sqrt)       # same but returns a list

# For loop
for (i in 1:4) {
  print(i * 3)
}

# If / else
a <- 5; b <- 10
if (a < b) { print("a is smaller") } else { print("b is smaller") }
```

```{=html}
<table class="fn-table">
  <tr><th>Function</th><th>What it does</th></tr>
  <tr><td>apply(X, 1, fun)</td><td>Apply fun to each row of matrix/dataframe</td></tr>
  <tr><td>apply(X, 2, fun)</td><td>Apply fun to each column</td></tr>
  <tr><td>sapply(x, fun)</td><td>Apply fun to each element of vector/list → vector</td></tr>
  <tr><td>lapply(x, fun)</td><td>Apply fun to each element → list</td></tr>
</table>
</div>
```

## Index Selection

```{=html}
<div class="ref-section">
<h3>which, %in%, is.na</h3>
```

```r
x <- c(2, 8, 3, 7, 1)

which(x > 5)          # c(2, 4)  — INDICES where condition is TRUE
x[which(x > 5)]       # c(8, 7)  — VALUES at those indices

c("a","b","c") %in% c("b","d")  # FALSE TRUE FALSE
                                 # — is each element in the right-hand set?

is.na(c(1, NA, 3))    # FALSE TRUE FALSE
sum(is.na(x))         # count of NA values
```

```{=html}
<table class="fn-table">
  <tr><th>Function / Operator</th><th>What it does</th></tr>
  <tr><td>which(condition)</td><td>Returns indices where condition is TRUE</td></tr>
  <tr><td>x %in% y</td><td>For each element of x: is it anywhere in y?</td></tr>
  <tr><td>is.na(x)</td><td>TRUE for each NA element</td></tr>
  <tr><td>na.omit(x)</td><td>Remove NA values from a vector or dataframe</td></tr>
</table>
</div>
```
